categories.label: Manufacturing
categories.blurb: Machines, quality and output on the factory floor.

categories.label: Quality control
categories.blurb: Check parts and products, from photos or from line readings.

templates.name: Machine failure warning
templates.question: Which machines are likely to break down in the next 7 days, so you can service them first?
templates.predicts: Will this machine fail in the next 7 days: yes or no, and how sure.
templates.row_means: One machine on one day.
templates.source: Your machine sensors or MES, plus the maintenance log
templates.balance: Failures are rare. Try to have at least 50 rows where the answer is yes.
tips: Use readings from before the failure, never from the day it broke.
One row per machine per day works better than one row per machine.
Leave machines out on days they were switched off.

columns.name: machine_type
columns.meaning: The model or family of the machine.

columns.name: air_temp_c
columns.meaning: Air temperature around the machine, in °C.

columns.name: speed_rpm
columns.meaning: How fast it turns, in turns per minute.

columns.name: tool_wear_min
columns.meaning: Minutes the current tool has been used.

columns.name: hours_run_week
columns.meaning: Hours it ran in the last 7 days.

columns.name: alarms_7d
columns.meaning: Alarms it raised in the last 7 days.

columns.name: age_years
columns.meaning: How old the machine is, in years.

columns.name: fails_within_7_days
columns.meaning: Did it fail in the 7 days after this day?

templates.name: Spot bad batches early
templates.question: Will this batch pass quality control, judged from the line settings while it is made?
templates.predicts: Pass or fail for each batch, before it reaches inspection.
templates.row_means: One batch.
templates.source: Line settings from the PLC or MES, plus QC results
templates.balance: Include failed batches too. A model that only sees passes cannot learn what a fail looks like.
tips: Use the settings recorded while the batch ran, not after.
Keep one supplier code per raw material as a category.

columns.name: supplier
columns.meaning: Supplier of the main raw material.

columns.name: material_lot_age_days
columns.meaning: Days since the material lot arrived.

columns.name: minutes_since_changeover
columns.meaning: Minutes since the line last changed product.

columns.name: defects_last_hour
columns.meaning: Defects found on the line in the hour before.

templates.name: Energy use per shift
templates.question: How many kWh will the next shift use, so you can plan load and cost?
templates.predicts: The energy one shift will use, in kWh.
templates.row_means: One shift on one line.
templates.source: Energy meters and the production plan
templates.balance: Include quiet shifts and busy ones, so the model sees the full range.
tips: Plan numbers like planned units are fine; actual numbers from after the shift are not.

columns.name: weekend
columns.meaning: Yes on a Saturday or Sunday.

templates.name: Why did the line stop?
templates.question: When a machine stops, what is the most likely cause, so the right person is called first?
templates.predicts: One cause: mechanical, electrical, material or operator.
templates.row_means: One stop on one machine.
templates.source: Downtime log from your MES, with the cause the technician wrote down
templates.balance: Try to have at least 50 stops for each cause.
tips: Use the alarm code and readings from the moment it stopped, not the repair notes.
Merge causes that mean the same thing, like "belt" and "belt worn".

columns.name: days_since_service
columns.meaning: Days since the machine was last serviced.

columns.name: material_changed
columns.meaning: Yes if a new material lot was loaded that shift.

templates.name: Batch yield
templates.question: What share of a batch will be good, from the settings and materials, before it runs?
templates.predicts: Good units as a percentage of the batch.
templates.row_means: One batch.
templates.source: Batch records and the production plan
templates.balance: Include poor batches too, so the model learns what drags yield down.
tips: Record the raw material lot or grade; it often explains most of the spread.

columns.name: material_grade
columns.meaning: Grade of the main raw material.

columns.name: days_since_service
columns.meaning: Days since the line was last serviced.

columns.name: yield_pct
columns.meaning: Good units as a % of the batch.

templates.name: Tool change due
templates.question: Should this cutting tool be changed before the next job, before it ruins parts?
templates.predicts: Change the tool now: yes or no.
templates.row_means: One tool before one job.
templates.source: CNC controller logs and tool change records
templates.balance: Rows where a change was needed are fewer; aim for 100 or more.
tips: Spindle load creeping up is usually the first sign; log it every job.

columns.name: feed_rate
columns.meaning: How fast the tool moves through material, in mm/min.

columns.name: minutes_since_change
columns.meaning: Minutes the tool has cut since it was fitted.

columns.name: change_needed
columns.meaning: Was the tool worn out at the next check?

templates.name: Surface defect check
templates.question: Look at a photo of a part and say if it is fine or has a scratch, dent or stain.
templates.predicts: One answer per photo: ok, scratch, dent or stain, with how sure.
templates.row_means: One photo of one part.
templates.source: A camera at the inspection station, or phone photos from inspectors
templates.balance: Defects are rare. Keep taking photos of defects until each folder has at least 100.
tips: Same camera, same angle, same light for every photo.
Fill the frame with the part; crop out the conveyor.
Include borderline parts that inspectors argued about.

folders.name: stain
folders.meaning: Parts with a stain or mark.

templates.name: Circuit board solder check
templates.question: Look at a close-up of a solder joint and say if it is good or which fault it has.
templates.predicts: Good, bridge, missing or cold joint, for each photo.
templates.row_means: One close-up photo of one joint.
templates.source: Your AOI machine images, or a microscope camera
templates.balance: At least 100 photos of each fault.
tips: Crop each photo to one joint; the model learns faster.
Keep the board the same way up in every photo.

templates.name: Weld seam inspection
templates.question: Check a photo of a weld for porosity, cracks or undercut before the part moves on.
templates.predicts: Good, porosity, crack or undercut, for each photo.
templates.row_means: One photo of one weld seam.
templates.source: Camera on the welding cell, or photos from the weld inspector
templates.balance: Cracks are rare; collect them over several weeks.
tips: Clean the seam before the photo; spatter confuses the model.
Use a diffuser so the metal does not glare.

templates.name: Packaging and label check
templates.question: Before boxes leave the line, check that the label is there, readable and the box is not torn.
templates.predicts: Ok, misprint, torn or no label, for each photo.
templates.row_means: One photo of one box or pack.
templates.source: A camera at the end of the packing line
templates.balance: You can stage bad examples on purpose: tear a few empty boxes, print a few bad labels.
tips: Photograph the side where the label goes, every time.

folders.name: misprint
folders.meaning: Label smudged, cut off or wrong.

templates.name: Fruit and produce grading
templates.question: Grade fruit or vegetables from a photo so sorting is the same on every shift.
templates.predicts: Grade A, grade B or reject, for each photo.
templates.row_means: One photo of one piece of produce.
templates.source: Photos from the sorting table
templates.balance: Have graders agree on the folders first; the model copies their judgement.
tips: Use a plain background in one colour.
Photograph both sides if bruises can be on either.

templates.name: Out of tolerance warning
templates.question: Will this machined part be out of tolerance, judged from the machine settings before measuring?
templates.predicts: Out of tolerance: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One part.
templates.source: CNC logs plus your CMM measurement results
templates.balance: Out-of-tolerance parts are rare; 100 or more makes the model useful.
tips: Room temperature matters for tight tolerances; log it.

columns.name: minutes_since_calibration
columns.meaning: Minutes since the machine was last calibrated.

templates.name: Lead scoring
templates.question: Which new leads are most likely to become customers, so sales calls them first?
templates.predicts: Will this lead become a customer: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One lead.
templates.source: Your CRM export, like HubSpot or Salesforce
templates.balance: Only use leads old enough to have a final answer, for example 90 days or older.
tips: Count activity from before the deal was decided, not after.
Group rare industries into "other" so each group has enough rows.

columns.name: pages_viewed
columns.meaning: Pages they looked at on your site.

columns.name: annual_revenue_musd
columns.meaning: The company's yearly revenue, in millions of dollars.

columns.name: site_visits_30d
columns.meaning: Visits to your website in the last 30 days.

columns.name: days_since_first_touch
columns.meaning: Days since the lead first came in.

columns.name: uses_competitor
columns.meaning: Yes if they already use a competitor's product.

columns.name: budget_known
columns.meaning: How much budget they said they have, in thousands; 0 if not said.

templates.name: Deal win chance
templates.question: How likely is each open deal to close, so the forecast is honest?
templates.predicts: Will this deal be won: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One deal.
templates.source: Closed deals from your CRM
templates.balance: Use deals that are already won or lost. Open deals have no answer yet.
tips: Take each deal as it looked at the same stage, for example when the proposal was sent.

columns.name: decision_maker_met
columns.meaning: Yes if you have met the person who signs.

columns.name: days_since_last_contact
columns.meaning: Days since you last heard from the buyer.

templates.name: Account renewal risk
templates.question: Which business accounts may not renew, so success can step in early?
templates.predicts: Will this account renew: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One account at 90 days before renewal.
templates.source: Billing system plus product usage
templates.balance: Accounts that left are usually few. 30 or more is a good start.
tips: Measure usage in the 30 days before the snapshot date.

columns.name: active_users_30d
columns.meaning: People who used it in the last 30 days.

columns.name: tickets_90d
columns.meaning: Support tickets in the last 90 days.

columns.name: months_customer
columns.meaning: How long they have been a customer, in months.

columns.name: nps
columns.meaning: Their latest recommend score, from -100 to 100.

columns.name: late_payments_12m
columns.meaning: Invoices paid late in the last 12 months.

columns.name: champion_left
columns.meaning: Yes if your main contact there has left.

templates.name: Upsell chance
templates.question: Which customers are ready for a bigger plan or more seats, so account managers call the right ones?
templates.predicts: Will this account upgrade in the next 90 days: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One account on one date.
templates.source: Billing system plus product usage
templates.balance: Upgrades are usually few; 50 or more is a good start.
tips: Seat usage near 100% is a strong sign; include it as a percentage.

columns.name: months_customer
columns.meaning: How long they have been a customer.

columns.name: meetings_90d
columns.meaning: Meetings with your team in 90 days.

columns.name: tickets_90d
columns.meaning: Support tickets in the last 90 days.

columns.name: hit_plan_limit
columns.meaning: Yes if they reached a limit of their plan.

columns.name: active_users_30d
columns.meaning: People who used it in the last 30 days.

templates.name: Campaign response
templates.question: Which accounts will respond to the next campaign, so you send it to fewer people and get more replies?
templates.predicts: Will this contact respond: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One contact in one past campaign.
templates.source: Your marketing tool, like HubSpot, Mailchimp or Marketo
templates.balance: Replies are rare. Use several past campaigns to get 200 or more.
tips: A reply, a meeting or a form fill all count as yes; pick one rule and keep it.

columns.name: past_responses
columns.meaning: Times they answered an earlier campaign.

columns.name: existing_customer
columns.meaning: Yes if they already buy from you.

columns.name: site_visits_30d
columns.meaning: Visits to your website in the last 30 days.

templates.name: Best way to reach
templates.question: For each contact, which channel gets an answer: email, a call, LinkedIn or an event invite?
templates.predicts: One channel: email, call, linkedin or event.
templates.row_means: One contact, with the channel that first got a reply.
templates.source: CRM activity history
templates.balance: Try to have at least 100 contacts for each channel.
tips: Only use contacts who replied; the answer is the channel they replied on.

columns.name: linkedin_connected
columns.meaning: Connected to your team on LinkedIn?

columns.name: calls_answered_90d
columns.meaning: Calls of yours they picked up in the last 90 days.

columns.name: whatsapp_replies_90d
columns.meaning: WhatsApp messages they answered in the last 90 days.

columns.name: best_channel
columns.meaning: Channel that first got a reply.

templates.name: Next-quarter revenue per account
templates.question: How much will each account spend next quarter, so sales targets and forecasts are realistic?
templates.predicts: Revenue from this account next quarter.
templates.row_means: One account in one quarter.
templates.source: Billing history plus the CRM pipeline
templates.balance: At least four quarters of history per account helps.
tips: Use open pipeline as it stood at the start of the quarter, not the end.

columns.name: seats
columns.meaning: Paid seats at the start of the quarter.

columns.name: revenue_same_q_last_year
columns.meaning: Revenue in the same quarter a year ago.

columns.name: open_pipeline
columns.meaning: Value of open deals for this account.

columns.name: active_users_30d
columns.meaning: Active users in the last 30 days.

columns.name: months_customer
columns.meaning: How long they have been a customer, in months.

columns.name: tickets_90d
columns.meaning: Support tickets in the last 90 days.

columns.name: price_change_pct
columns.meaning: Change in their price this quarter, in %.

columns.name: renewal_this_q
columns.meaning: Yes if their contract renews this quarter.

templates.name: Who to visit next
templates.question: Which customers and leads should a salesperson visit tomorrow, this week or in the next N days, because they are likeliest to order or move forward?
templates.predicts: Will this customer or lead order, or move a deal forward, within the next N days: yes or no, and how likely. Sort the accounts by that chance to plan the visits.
templates.row_means: One customer or lead on one planning day, for one window of days ahead.
templates.source: CRM accounts and visit log, joined with orders from your ERP or billing system
templates.balance: Most accounts don't order in a short window; 100 or more yes rows is a good start.
tips: Make a row for each account on each past planning day, for each window you plan with, such as 1, 7 and 30 days. Then one model answers for tomorrow, next week and next month.
Only use what was known on the planning day: orders, visits and quotes up to that day, and whether they ordered within the window after it.

To plan, use Score a list on every customer and lead in the territory, with today's values and the window you want, and visit the likeliest first. Scoring from a database can run every day, so the list is ready each morning.
Leave days_since_last_order and the order columns empty for leads; account_type tells the model they are leads.

columns.name: days_since_last_order
columns.meaning: Days since their last order, on the planning day.

columns.name: avg_days_between_orders
columns.meaning: Their usual gap between orders, in days.

columns.name: order_total_last_90d
columns.meaning: Money ordered in the 90 days before.

columns.name: open_quotes
columns.meaning: Quotes sent and not yet answered.

columns.name: visit_window_days
columns.meaning: How many days ahead the row looks: 1 for tomorrow, 7 for the next week, up to 30.

columns.name: distance_km
columns.meaning: How far it is from the sales office, in km.

columns.name: buys_in_window
columns.meaning: Did they order, or did the lead's deal move forward, within that many days after the planning day?

templates.name: Days until the next order
templates.question: How many days until each customer orders again, so the visit lands just before they need to reorder?
templates.predicts: The number of days until the customer's next order. Visit those due within your planning window.
templates.row_means: One customer on the day of one of their orders.
templates.source: Order history from your ERP or billing system
templates.balance: Include customers who order often and rarely, so it learns both.
tips: Make a row for each order, with what was known that day and the days until the customer's next order.
Leave out each customer's latest order: its next order hasn't happened yet.

columns.name: avg_days_between_orders
columns.meaning: Their usual gap between orders, in days.

columns.name: days_since_last_order
columns.meaning: Days since the order before this one.

columns.name: on_promo
columns.meaning: Yes if a promotion was running when they ordered.

columns.name: stock_weeks_left
columns.meaning: Weeks of stock they said they had left; blank if not known.

columns.name: days_to_next_order
columns.meaning: Days from this order to their next one.

templates.name: Chance they order within N days
templates.question: How likely is each customer to order again within the next N days, so salespeople visit the ones about to reorder, for tomorrow, this week or this month?
templates.predicts: The chance the customer orders within the number of days you ask, from 0 to 100%. Ask with within_days set to 1, 7, 30 or any other number.
templates.row_means: One customer since one of their orders: what was known that day, how many days were watched after it, and whether they ordered again in that time.
templates.source: Order history from your ERP or billing system, with customer details from your CRM
templates.balance: Include customers who haven't reordered yet, with no and the days since their last order; leaving them out makes everyone look faster than they are.
tips: Make a row for each order. days_watched is the days until the next order when there was one (reordered yes), or the days until today when there wasn't (reordered no).
Unlike a yes or no model, one model answers for any window: ask with within_days 1 for tomorrow, 7 for the next week.
To plan visits, use Score a list on every customer with today's values and the window you want, and visit the likeliest first.

columns.name: avg_days_between_orders
columns.meaning: Their usual gap between orders, in days.

columns.name: open_quotes
columns.meaning: Quotes sent and not yet answered.

columns.name: days_watched
columns.meaning: Days from this order to the next one, or to today if there is none yet.

columns.name: reordered
columns.meaning: Did they order again within days_watched?

templates.name: Products to offer each customer
templates.question: Which products should a salesperson offer each customer, from what they and customers like them already buy?
templates.predicts: The 10 products each customer is likeliest to want, best first. A new customer or a lead gets the products most customers buy.
templates.row_means: One order line: a customer and a product they bought.
templates.source: Order lines from your ERP or billing system
templates.balance: Customers with a few orders each help most; products bought only once or twice are rarely suggested.
tips: Ask with a customer_id to get their list. Leave out products they buy every time if you only want new ideas to offer.
Use quantity, or leave it out to count each order line once.
Teach it again every week or month as new orders come in, so it keeps up with what customers buy.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.meaning: Who bought: the customer's number in your system.

columns.name: quantity
columns.meaning: How many they bought on this line.

columns.name: product
columns.meaning: The product they bought: its code or name.

templates.name: Products bought together
templates.question: Which products are bought in the same order as this one far more often than chance, to offer next to it or place side by side?
templates.predicts: For any product, the 10 products that go with it most, best first. A product it hasn't seen gets the products most orders hold.
templates.row_means: One order line: an order and a product in it.
templates.source: Order lines from your ERP, point of sale or billing system
templates.balance: Orders of two or more lines teach it; a pair bought together in fewer than 3 orders is not counted.
tips: Ask with a product to get what goes with it. Score the whole product list to see every product's companions at once.
Give it order ids, not customer ids, so it learns what is bought in one go; with customer ids it learns what the same customer buys over time instead.
Teach it again every month as orders come in, so it keeps up with the range.

columns.name: order_id
columns.meaning: The order the line belongs to: its number in your system.

columns.name: quantity
columns.meaning: How many they bought on this line.

columns.name: product
columns.meaning: The product on the line: its code or name.

templates.name: Products nearby customers like them buy
templates.question: Which products should a salesperson offer a customer or lead, from what businesses of the same kind within N km already buy?
templates.predicts: The 10 products that customers of the same category within the distance you ask buy most, best first, leaving out what this customer already buys.
templates.row_means: One order line: a customer, its category and place, and a product it bought.
templates.source: Order lines from your ERP joined with customer addresses and categories from your CRM
templates.balance: Have at least 20 customers in each category; a category with fewer gets the products all customers buy.
tips: Ask with a customer_id and a radius_km, such as 5 for a city district or 50 for a region. Leave radius_km out and it uses a distance that reaches about 10 customers of the same kind.
For a lead, leave customer_id out and give its customer_category, latitude and longitude.
Latitude and longitude are in degrees, as maps show them. Geocode addresses once and keep them in your CRM.
Use Score a list with a salesperson's route for the day to get suggestions for every stop at once.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.meaning: Who bought: the customer's number in your system.

columns.name: customer_category
columns.meaning: What kind of business the customer is.

columns.name: latitude
columns.meaning: Where the customer is: latitude in degrees.

columns.name: longitude
columns.meaning: Where the customer is: longitude in degrees.

columns.name: quantity
columns.meaning: How many they bought on this line.

columns.name: product
columns.meaning: The product they bought: its code or name.

templates.name: Best next step for a lead
templates.question: For each lead or open deal, what should the salesperson do next: call, email, visit, demo, send a quote or offer a discount?
templates.predicts: The next steps ranked from likeliest to move the lead forward to least, with the chance each gives.
templates.row_means: One step a salesperson took with a lead or deal, and whether it moved forward.
templates.source: CRM activity log
templates.balance: Have at least 50 rows for each step; a step tried rarely can't be judged well.
tips: Log every step, the ones that worked and the ones that didn't; it compares them in similar situations.
It learns best when salespeople sometimes try different steps in similar situations, not always the same one.
Count a step as a success when the lead or deal moved to the next stage within 14 days.

columns.name: account_type
columns.meaning: New lead, or an existing customer with a new deal.

columns.name: stage
columns.meaning: Where the lead or deal is.

columns.name: days_in_stage
columns.meaning: Days it has sat in that stage.

columns.name: days_since_last_contact
columns.meaning: Days since anyone talked to them.

columns.name: emails_opened_30d
columns.meaning: Your emails they opened in 30 days.

columns.name: step_success
columns.meaning: Did the lead or deal move to the next stage within 14 days?

templates.name: First product for a lead
templates.question: Which product line should a salesperson pitch first to a new lead, from customers like them?
templates.predicts: One product line, with how likely each is.
templates.row_means: One customer, with the product line they bought first.
templates.source: CRM accounts joined with each customer's first order
templates.balance: Try to have at least 100 customers for each product line.
tips: Use what you knew about each customer before their first order, as you would for a new lead.
For customers with order history, Products to offer each customer usually suggests better.

columns.name: sites
columns.meaning: How many sites or branches they run.

columns.name: site_visits_30d
columns.meaning: Visits to your website in the last 30 days.

columns.name: pages_most_read
columns.meaning: The product section they read most on your site.

columns.name: product_line
columns.meaning: Product line of their first order.

templates.name: Leads that look like your best customers
templates.question: Which leads and small accounts look most like your best customers, so salespeople visit the most promising first?
templates.predicts: How alike each customer or lead is to your best customers, from 0 to 100. Score your whole lead list and sort it.
templates.row_means: One customer or lead, as it is today.
templates.source: CRM accounts, with sales from your ERP or invoices
templates.balance: Mark at least 30 best customers yes, for example the top 20% by revenue or margin. Leads you haven't sold to are no.
tips: Decide what makes a customer best before you start: revenue, margin, how long they stay, or all three.
Use only what you also know about a lead: industry, size, area, channel. Leave out sales figures, which leads don't have yet.
Score the lead list afterwards; anything above 50 is as alike as a typical best customer.

columns.name: channel
columns.meaning: How they buy or would buy.

columns.name: outlets
columns.meaning: How many shops or sites they run.

columns.name: years_in_business
columns.meaning: How long the business has run, in years.

columns.name: has_website
columns.meaning: Yes if they have a website.

columns.name: best_customer
columns.meaning: Yes for your best customers, no for everyone else, leads included.

templates.name: Product lines each customer will buy
templates.question: Which of your product lines will each customer buy next quarter, so salespeople bring the right catalogue and samples?
templates.predicts: The chance of each product line, apart from the others, so a customer can get several.
templates.row_means: One customer and one quarter: who they were before it, and every line they bought in it.
templates.source: ERP sales lines, grouped by customer and quarter
templates.balance: Each product line needs at least 10 rows with it and 10 without.
tips: Describe the customer as they were before the quarter, and list what they bought during it.
Separate the lines with a semicolon, like snacks; drinks. A quarter they bought nothing has an empty cell.
Use product lines or categories, not single products: 5 to 25 of them work best.

columns.name: revenue_last_q
columns.meaning: What they bought in the quarter before.

columns.name: lines_last_q
columns.meaning: How many product lines they bought in the quarter before.

columns.name: months_customer
columns.meaning: How long they have bought from you, in months.

columns.name: visits_last_q
columns.meaning: Sales visits in the quarter before.

columns.name: product_lines
columns.meaning: Every product line they bought in the quarter, separated by semicolons.

templates.name: Discount needed to close a deal
templates.question: How much does a discount raise the chance of winning this deal, and which discount keeps the most revenue?
templates.predicts: The chance of closing at each discount, with the discount that keeps the most revenue after what it gives away.
templates.row_means: One quote or deal that was won or lost, and the discount offered.
templates.source: CRM deals or quotes with their final discount
templates.balance: Have deals won and lost at several discounts, at least 30 at each.
tips: Use the discount in the final offer, in %.
Only closed deals: won or lost. Leave out ones still open.
It learns from what happened, so it can't know why a discount was given. If big discounts went to hard deals, read the effect with care.

columns.name: deal_size
columns.meaning: The quote's value before the discount.

columns.name: competitor_quoted
columns.meaning: Yes if a competitor also quoted.

columns.name: days_open
columns.meaning: Days since the quote was sent.

columns.name: existing_customer
columns.meaning: Yes if they already buy from you.

templates.name: Order size range
templates.question: How big will a customer's next order be, as a range you can plan stock and trucks with?
templates.predicts: The likeliest order size, with a low and a high that hold about 8 in 10 real orders.
templates.row_means: One order, and what was known about the customer before it.
templates.source: ERP or order system
templates.balance: Orders of every size, small and big, from many customers.
tips: The range is wider where orders swing more; that is information, not an error.
Use what was known before the order: past orders, season, promotion.
Plan for the high end when running out costs more than spare stock.

columns.name: avg_order_last_6m
columns.meaning: Their average order in the last 6 months, in units.

columns.name: on_promo
columns.meaning: Yes if a promotion runs when they order.

templates.name: Duplicate customer accounts
templates.question: Which customer accounts are the same business entered twice, like PT Maju Jaya and Maju Jaya, PT, so the CRM and credit limits stay clean?
templates.predicts: For each account or new lead, the existing accounts that are likely the same business, best match first, or no match.
templates.row_means: One customer account.

templates.question: Which shoppers are about to leave without paying, so you can show help or a reminder in time?
templates.predicts: Will this cart be left without buying: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One shopping session with something in the cart.
templates.source: Your web shop or app analytics
templates.balance: Use sessions from every day of the week, sales days and quiet ones.
tips: Use what was known while the shopper was still there, not whether they came back later.

columns.name: minutes_on_site
columns.meaning: Minutes on the site so far.

templates.name: Orders likely to be returned
templates.question: Which orders are likely to come back, so you can suggest another size or check the order before it ships?
templates.predicts: Will this order be returned: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One order.
templates.source: Your shop orders and the returns log
templates.balance: Only use orders older than your return window.
tips: Use what was known when the order was placed.

columns.name: sizes_in_order
columns.meaning: Sizes of the same item in the order.

columns.name: customer_return_rate_pct
columns.meaning: Share of their past orders they sent back, in %.

columns.name: first_order
columns.meaning: Yes if it's their first order.

templates.name: Spend in the next 12 months
templates.question: How much will each customer spend in the next year, so you know who is worth keeping and what to spend winning them?
templates.predicts: The money a customer will spend in the next 12 months.
templates.row_means: One customer, as they looked a year ago.
templates.source: Order history from your shop or loyalty programme
templates.balance: Include customers who spent nothing in the year after, with 0.
tips: Take the columns from a year ago and the spend from the year after, so the model learns to look ahead.

columns.name: spend_last_12m
columns.meaning: Money spent in the year before.

columns.name: member
columns.meaning: Yes if they're in the loyalty programme.

columns.name: spend_next_12m
columns.meaning: Money spent in the year after.

templates.name: Products to show each shopper
templates.question: Which products should the shop show each shopper on the home page or in an email, from what they and shoppers like them bought?
templates.predicts: The 10 products each shopper is likeliest to want, best first. A new shopper gets the products most shoppers buy.
templates.row_means: One purchase: a shopper and a product they bought.
templates.source: Order lines from your shop or loyalty programme
templates.balance: Shoppers with a few purchases each help most.
tips: Ask with a shopper_id to get their list.
Teach it again every week, so it keeps up with the season.

templates.name: Items in the same basket
templates.question: Which items end up in the same shopping basket far more often than chance, to place them side by side or bundle them?
templates.predicts: For any item, the 10 items that go with it most, best first.
templates.row_means: One basket line: a receipt and an item on it.
templates.source: Receipts from your point of sale or web shop
templates.balance: Baskets of two or more items teach it.
tips: Give it receipt ids, not shopper ids, so it learns what is bought in one go.
Teach it again every month as the range changes.

templates.name: What reviews are about
templates.question: Read each review and say what it's mainly about, so the right team sees the complaints that are theirs.
templates.predicts: Delivery, quality, size or price, for each review.
templates.row_means: One review.
templates.source: Reviews from your shop, app store or marketplace
templates.balance: Try to have at least 100 reviews for each topic.
tips: Keep the review as the customer wrote it; spelling mistakes are fine.

columns.name: review_text
examples: Stitching came apart after one wash
Runs small, order one size up
Cheaper in the shop next door

templates.name: Chance an invoice is paid within N days
templates.question: How likely is each open invoice to be paid within the next N days, so cash planning and reminders start with the right ones?
templates.predicts: The chance the invoice is paid within the number of days you ask, from 0 to 100%. Ask with within_days set to 7, 30 or any other number.
templates.row_means: One invoice: what was known when it was sent, how many days were watched after it, and whether it was paid in that time.
templates.source: Invoices and payments from your accounting system
templates.balance: Include invoices still unpaid, with no and the days since they were sent.
tips: days_watched is the days until payment when it was paid (paid yes), or the days until today when it wasn't (paid no).
Ask with within_days 30 to see which invoices to chase this month.

columns.name: payment_terms_days
columns.meaning: Days the customer has to pay.

columns.name: customer_avg_days_late
columns.meaning: How late this customer usually pays, in days.

columns.name: disputed
columns.meaning: Yes if the customer questioned the invoice.

columns.name: days_watched
columns.meaning: Days from sending to payment, or to today if it isn't paid yet.

templates.name: Expense claims to check
templates.question: Which expense claims look wrong and deserve a second look before they're paid?
templates.predicts: Should this claim be checked: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One expense claim.
templates.source: Your expense system, with the claims that were rejected or corrected
templates.balance: Wrong claims are rare. Use at least a year of claims so there are enough of them.
tips: Use the claims your finance team already checked, with what they decided.

columns.name: receipt_attached
columns.meaning: Yes if a receipt is attached.

columns.name: weekend
columns.meaning: Yes if the spend was on a weekend.

columns.name: days_after_spend
columns.meaning: Days between the spend and the claim.

columns.name: claims_this_month
columns.meaning: Claims the person made this month.

templates.name: Sort bank transactions
templates.question: Read each bank or card transaction and file it under the right account, so bookkeeping isn't done by hand.
templates.predicts: Rent, salaries, supplies, travel or software, for each transaction.
templates.row_means: One bank or card transaction.
templates.source: Bank statements, with the account your bookkeeper chose
templates.balance: Try to have at least 100 transactions for each account.
tips: Keep the description exactly as the bank wrote it.

columns.name: description
columns.meaning: The text on the bank statement.
examples: TRF PT GEDUNG MAJU SEWA NOV

templates.name: Days late on a payment
templates.question: How many days late will a customer pay this invoice, so your cash forecast uses real dates instead of the due date?
templates.predicts: The days after the due date the invoice will be paid; 0 means on time.
templates.row_means: One paid invoice.
templates.source: Invoices and payments from your accounting system
templates.balance: Include invoices paid on time, with 0.
tips: Use what was known when the invoice was sent.

columns.name: payment_terms_days
columns.meaning: Days the customer has to pay.

columns.name: customer_avg_days_late
columns.meaning: How late this customer usually pays, in days.

columns.name: invoices_open
columns.meaning: Other unpaid invoices of this customer.

columns.name: month_end
columns.meaning: Yes if the due date is in the last week of a month.

columns.name: days_late
columns.meaning: Days after the due date it was paid.

templates.name: Salary range for a role
templates.question: What should a role pay, as a range, so offers are fair and in line with the people already doing similar work?
templates.predicts: The likeliest monthly salary, with a low and a high that hold about 8 in 10 people in similar roles.
templates.row_means: One person, with their role and their salary.
templates.source: Your HR or payroll system
templates.balance: People at every level and in every department.
tips: Leave out names, gender, age and anything else a salary must not depend on.
Check the range against market data before you use it for offers.

columns.name: years_experience
columns.meaning: Years of work in this field.

templates.name: Long absence risk
templates.question: Who is likely to be off for more than a week in the next three months, so managers can check in and plan cover early?
templates.predicts: Will this person be off for more than a week: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One person at the start of a quarter.
templates.source: Your HR system and the absence log
templates.balance: Use several quarters, so there are enough long absences.
tips: Use it to offer help and plan cover, not to judge people.
Leave out health details; the model doesn't need them.

columns.name: days_off_last_year
columns.meaning: Days off sick in the year before.

columns.name: long_absence
columns.meaning: Were they off for more than a week in the quarter?

templates.name: Chance someone leaves within N months
templates.question: How likely is each person to leave within the next N months, so managers have the right talk in time?
templates.predicts: The chance the person leaves within the number of months you ask, from 0 to 100%. Ask with within_days set to 3, 6, 12 or any other number of months.
templates.row_means: One person since one review: what was known that day, how many months were watched after it, and whether they left in that time.
templates.source: Your HR system, with leaving dates
templates.balance: Include people who are still here, with no and the months since their review.
tips: months_watched is the months until they left when they did (left yes), or the months until today when they didn't (left no).
Use it to start conversations, not to make decisions about people.

columns.name: manager_changes_2y
columns.meaning: New managers in the last two years.

columns.name: months_watched
columns.meaning: Months from this review until they left, or until today.

templates.name: Courses to suggest to each person
templates.question: Which training courses should each person see next, from what they and colleagues like them took?
templates.predicts: The 10 courses each person is likeliest to take, best first. A new starter gets the courses most people take.
templates.row_means: One course someone finished.
templates.source: Your learning system
templates.balance: People who finished a few courses each help most.
tips: Ask with an employee_id to get their list.

templates.name: Why people leave
templates.question: Read what people said when they left and sort it by the main reason, so you can see what to fix first.
templates.predicts: Pay, manager, growth or workload, for each answer.
templates.row_means: One exit interview or leaving survey.
templates.source: Exit interviews or leaving surveys
templates.balance: Try to have at least 50 answers for each reason.
tips: Remove names before you upload.

columns.name: answer
columns.meaning: What they said about why they're leaving.
examples: No path to the next level

templates.name: Delivery time range
templates.question: How many hours will a delivery take, as a range you can tell customers and plan routes with?
templates.predicts: The likeliest hours from pick-up to delivery, with a low and a high that hold about 8 in 10 real deliveries.
templates.row_means: One delivery.
templates.source: Your transport or courier system
templates.balance: Deliveries near and far, on quiet days and busy ones.
tips: Promise the high end when being late costs more than being early.

templates.name: Stock-out warning
templates.question: Which items will run out in a store or warehouse next week, so you can reorder or move stock now?
templates.predicts: Will this item run out next week: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One item in one location in one week.
templates.source: Your stock and sales records
templates.balance: Use many weeks and locations, so there are enough stock-outs.
tips: Use stock at the start of the week and sales before it.

columns.name: stock_on_hand
columns.meaning: Units on the shelf at the start of the week.

columns.name: avg_weekly_sales
columns.meaning: Average units sold a week, last 4 weeks.

columns.name: days_to_next_delivery
columns.meaning: Days until the next delivery comes.

columns.name: on_promo
columns.meaning: Yes if there's a promotion next week.

columns.name: supplier_late_rate_pct
columns.meaning: Share of the supplier's deliveries that came late, in %.

columns.name: ran_out
columns.meaning: Did it run out that week?

templates.name: Best carrier for a shipment
templates.question: Which carrier will get a shipment there on time, so each one goes with the right company?
templates.predicts: The carrier that delivered shipments like this best, for each shipment.
templates.row_means: One shipment that arrived on time, with the carrier that took it.
templates.source: Your shipping records
templates.balance: Try to have at least 100 on-time shipments for each carrier.
tips: Use only shipments that arrived on time and undamaged, so the model learns what each carrier does well.

columns.name: cash_on_delivery
columns.meaning: Yes if the receiver pays on delivery.

templates.name: Why a delivery failed
templates.question: Read the driver's note on a failed delivery and say why it failed, so the next try is planned right.
templates.predicts: Nobody home, wrong address, refused or no access, for each note.
templates.row_means: One failed delivery.
templates.source: Driver notes from your delivery app
templates.balance: Try to have at least 100 notes for each reason.
tips: Keep the note as the driver wrote it; short is fine.

columns.name: driver_note
examples: Customer said they did not order it
Gate locked, guard would not let me in

templates.name: Pallet load check
templates.question: Look at a photo of a loaded pallet and say if it's fine to ship, badly wrapped or leaning.
templates.predicts: One answer per photo: ok, bad wrap or leaning, with how sure.
templates.row_means: One photo of one pallet.
templates.source: A camera at the loading dock, or phone photos from the team
templates.balance: Keep taking photos of bad pallets until each folder has at least 100.
tips: Take the photo from the same side and height each time.
Get the whole pallet in the frame.

templates.name: Unhappy after a ticket
templates.question: Which customers are likely to rate their support badly, so a team lead can step in before the ticket closes?
templates.predicts: Will the customer give a bad rating: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One closed ticket with a rating.
templates.source: Your helpdesk, with satisfaction ratings
templates.balance: Only use tickets where the customer left a rating.
tips: Use what was known before the ticket closed.

columns.name: reopened
columns.meaning: Yes if the customer reopened it.

columns.name: transferred
columns.meaning: Times it moved to another team.

columns.name: bad_rating
columns.meaning: Did they give 1 or 2 out of 5?

templates.name: Time to solve a ticket
templates.question: How many hours will a ticket take to solve, so you can tell customers honestly and spot the ones that will miss their deadline?
templates.predicts: The hours from opening to solved.
templates.row_means: One solved ticket.
templates.source: Your helpdesk
templates.balance: Quick tickets and long ones, from every team.
tips: Use what was known when the ticket came in.

columns.name: open_tickets_in_queue
columns.meaning: Tickets already waiting in the team's queue.

templates.name: How urgent a message is
templates.question: Read what the customer wrote and say how urgent it is, so the most pressing tickets are answered first.
templates.predicts: Low, normal or urgent, for each ticket.
templates.row_means: One ticket.
templates.source: Your helpdesk, with the priority your team gave
templates.balance: Urgent tickets are rare; try to have at least 100.
tips: Use the customer's first message only.

columns.name: message
examples: Could you add dark mode one day?
How do I change my invoice address?
Our whole team can't log in and we have a launch today

templates.name: Customers who may leave after support
templates.question: Which customers who contacted support are likely to cancel in the next month, so someone reaches out first?
templates.predicts: Will this customer cancel within a month: yes or no, and how likely.
templates.row_means: One customer after a support contact.
templates.source: Your helpdesk and billing system
templates.balance: Only use contacts more than a month old.
tips: Use what was known when the ticket closed.

columns.name: tickets_90d
columns.meaning: Tickets they opened in the last 90 days.

columns.name: solved_first_time
columns.meaning: Yes if the first answer solved it.

columns.name: hours_to_solve
columns.meaning: Hours to solve the last ticket.

columns.name: bad_rating
columns.meaning: Yes if they rated the last ticket badly.

columns.name: cancelled
columns.meaning: Did they cancel within a month?
